Representation Act, 1985

The House resumed consideration of the Motion of Mr. Hnatyshyn that Bill C-74, an Act to amend the Constitution Act, 1867 and the Electoral Boundaries Readjustment Act and to provide for certain matters in relation to the 1981 decennial census, be read the third time and passed; and the amendment of Mr. Prud'homme (p. 9258).
At one o'clock the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon (Mr. Epp) had the floor and had five minutes remaining. The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon.

Mr. Speaker, when we rose at one o'clock for the lunch break, I was exploring the way in which the Government in pushing through this redistribution Bill is demonstrating tyrannist tendencies which when the Opposition in the last Parliament it made much of. 1 was exploring the way in which the redistribution Bill knocks out one of the very cornerstones of the representational system that we have observed since Confederation in using the population of Quebec and a specified number of seats, namely, 75, to go to 79 as the basis for deciding how many representatives other provinces should have and how large the Parliament of Canada should be.
It is specifically the change that has taken place in that particular relationship that is the basis for the motion to refer to committee the Bill that is before us this afternoon. The motion to refer the Bill to the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for further consideration of Clause 2 is what this amendment speaks to. It is about that I want to say a little more.
If we take a look at Part I of Bill C-74, we note the assignment of a certain number of seats, that is to say 279 as the basis to be used in dividing into the total population of Canada for the number of seats.
In rule 3 we read:
If the total number of Members that would be assigned to any province by the application of rule 1 is greater than the total number assigned to that province by the last preceding readjustment of the representation of that province made in accordance with this Act, the number of additional Members that would be so assigned shall, unless the number of additional Members is one, be reduced so that the actual number assigned is equal to one-half of the additional number that would be so assigned plus, where the number of additional Members that would be so assigned is an odd number in excess of one, one other Member.
It is this rule 3 which represents a deflation of the proper representation of Members in the House of Commons. It is here that the residents, Canadian citizens, living in the provinces of Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia have the clearest grievance with the Government. It is here that their expectation that population migration in Canada-adding to the numbers-should lead to proportionate increase in the number of Members they have in the House of Commons. It is here that that expectation is violated.

December 17, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
A Government that is obsessed with deficit reduction, withholding the line on expenditures wherever it can, is a Government that is prepared to violate the principles of the Canadian Constitution. That is what the Government is proposing in this Bill. The astounding thing is that Members who have been so outspoken in the past when in opposition in defence of Parliament, who present themselves often as the only ones who speak for Parliament, are now prepared to do something as fundamental as violating the structure of Parliament and are rejecting the right of people province by province where there is movement to see additional Members. They are quite prepared to see those expectations blasted and the Constitution of the country violated in these areas. The result for Members in northern Ontario is that the movement to Metro Toronto and to other areas, which deserves recognition, will lead to some readjustment of seats. We in northern Ontario do not look forward to a worsening of our representation or a violation of the rights of citizens to be represented properly in Parliament. We do not look forward to seeing that right violated by a penny-pinching Government which refuses to tax properly and cannot hold back on expenditures in other areas, to save a few hundreds of thousands of dollars by keeping down the growth of the Parliament of Canada; by a Government which is prepared to sacrifice principle in the Constitution of the country for budgetary reasons; by a Government which deserves to be turfed out by the people if they only had a chance.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret to interrupt the Hon. Member but his time has expired. There is still the period provided for questions and comments. Since there are no questions or comments, I will recognize the Right Hon. Leader of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition on debate.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is always good to see you in the chair. I wish you, and through you other Members of the House, the best of the Christmas season. It seems to be the quietest time to do it.
The proposal of the Government to impose closure on Bill C-74, an Act which in effect amends the Constitution of the country with regard to the number of Members who have the right to sit in this Chamber, cuts very deeply into the ability of the House to represent adequately the people of Canada. The House of Commons, its make-up, its essence and how we operate should not be tampered with in a careless, callous and cavalier fashion.
I warn those who sit on all sides of the House, particularly those who sit on the back-benches of the Conservative Government, to take heed and pay close attention to what the Government is attempting to do, because it affects all of us and our ability to represent adequately the people who did us the honour of sending us to the House. I look across to those benches and I see one or two Members who happen to know something about the Bill. Perhaps one of them is delegated as a hit man later this afternoon; we will see what he wants to do.
This is about the fifteenth time I have spoken on a Bill or a motion.
Unlike the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney).

Yes, unlike the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) who has spoken only twice-once on Leaders' day and once, for 15 minutes, to give us his vague ambiguities on free trade. 1 say to the Conservative back-benches and to the book-ends which surround us that they ought to be speaking on a Bill of this importance. They ought to be speaking as well on some of the Bills and other measures against which closure has been applied. I will speak to that. I think it is relevant to this third reading, because we are under the hammer of closure when we speak in the House and before Your Honour. We do not hear much over there. We do not hear much from these silent, invisible, anonymous men and women who pose as back-benchers in the Conservative Party.
This is the first time in the history of the House that a Government has made redistribution a partisan issue. At all times previously, redistribution, a measure to redivide the seats of the House of Commons, has been done in a non-partisan, impartial manner. There was all-Party agreement, in fact for 30 years. I can recall our Leader in the Senate, the Hon. Allan MacEachen, negotiating the deal with the late John George Diefenbaker, who was very close to Your Honour. 1 had the privilege of knowing him well. That accord made by Mr. Diefenbaker and Mr. MacEachen held over successive redistributions in a non-partisan fashion for the last quarter century. Under the terms of the agreement worked out by all Parties in the House, that formula, technically called the amalgam formula, but familiarly known to those of us who have been in the House for a number of years as the Diefenbaker-MacEachen formula, provided for an orderly adjustment in seat distribution following every census.
Following the 1981 census, the wheels were set in motion once again. All the work had been done, the commissioners were appointed, hearings were held, maps for the various constituencies across Canada were redrawn, and the proposals were being brought back for final agreement in the House. At that time only a short debate was required to complete that process. Suddenly, out of nowhere, out of the magic confines of the back rooms of the Conservative Party, the Government decided to change all the rules in the middle of the game.
Why?

Yes, that question might well be put. All that was required was a short, conclusive debate in the House of Commons. However, the Government reopened the matter in its partisan and insidious greed and produced a White Paper. That paper went to committee-all the work had been done but it was reopened-where many changes were discussed. Then the Government introduced Bill C-74 which was proposed in the White Paper. However, the Bill reflected the White Paper completely. None of the changes discussed in committee by all Parties were reflected or incorporated in the Bill. No account was taken of the argu-
December 17, 1985

merits made in committee to improve the redistribution principle.
1 believe the Bill before the House is a bad Bill in principle. It ends the redistribution process which is already under way, ready to function and needing only a short debate to conclude it and to legitimize it. It starts off another whole round of hearings and discussions.
I have heard the arguments of Government members. They want to save money. They say Parliament is too expensive. I venture to say that we get better value for Parliament than we are getting from this Government.
Hear, hear!

Under your administration, Sir, we get better value for dollars than we are getting for ministerial staffs and a bloated Prime Minister's Office.
We were told that increasing the membership to 310 Members would be estimated to cost $90 million over the next 10 years. The government proposal will cost an extra $41.7 million. We have here a saving over what had been worked out by all-Party agreement as against this proposal now before Your Honour, of $48.3 million over that period or $4.8 million per year.
When we look at the budget of the Prime Minister's Office, it is $7 million for 1985-86. That does not include other ministerial staff. It far exceeds the potential saving between what was agreed upon by all Parties and the cost envisaged by the Bill. This so-called great economizing measure is proposed by a Government which threw away $1 billion on a tax deal for Gulf Oil, a Government which blew another $1 billion to $2 billion on the first bank bankruptcy in the country for 60 years, a Government which does not know what the words competence, good management and good husbanding mean. It comes to the House and tries to tinker with the democratic process by painting a phoney argument for economy; that is what we have before us. I know the people of Canada want money for value-
Value for money.

Value for money, thank you. Let us look at the way Parliament works, generally speaking, with the reforms which have been introduced by our colleague on the Conservative benches, the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath). We will look at those reforms very carefully. We are trying to give the people of Canada value for money in the way we operate the House. However, you cannot put a price on democracy. You cannot justify a partisan measure overriding a non-partisan piece of work that was ready to be implemented on the phoney grounds of economy.

the Chief Electoral Officer. It will be just weeks or months before the usual expiry of a term of a majority Government. Bring it on.

speechtext: You were leading 11 per cent in the polls. What happened then?

The last time the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) and I were here in the Chamber alone-there is usually a great audience on both sides of the House when we speak-the Minister of Justice was bringing in his so-called reform of the Senate. That was a great measure and he had a head of steam. However, it is an empty engine right now, puffing and huffing-

Just weeks or months before a general election these boundaries will finally come into effect if this Bill is passed in the House. There will be mass confusion in the camps of all three political parties as we attempt to find out under which boundaries we will be working. If an election is called early, it will be the current boundaries. Will it be the boundaries agreed to under the amalgam method or Diefenbaker-MacEachen formula or will it be the new Tory boundaries-the new gerrymander boundaries? Will we be operating under the new artistically geographically manipulated boundaries?
The cost of the new Tory boundaries is approximately $5 million or $6 million which is in addition to that which is already spent.

Mr. Speaker, the most important thing this Bill does is to take away from the House its right to discuss the redistribution of electoral districts. From now on, all decisions on the subject will be taken by a committee, not by this House and not before Your Honour, Mr. Speaker, and the real reason why the Government wants to bring down the hammer of closure on debate is because it wants to have this Bill adopted. In fact, its reasons are very simple.
First of all, the Government wants to appoint 295 new Conservative returning officers, and since the number of

December 17, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
vacancies is very limited, the Prime Minister has found a way to get around this by creating 295 new jobs. All he has to do is have the legislation adopted and limit debate. What a nice Christmas present for 295 party faithful! What a nice Christmas present indeed!
And the second reason is that the Government wants to redistribute electoral districts to its own advantage. It has played around with the seats and manipulated the geographical boundaries of our ridings. They are going to analyze the election results, poll by poll to locate their supporters. They are going to isolate those who voted against them, but as far as we are concerned, Mr. Speaker, we cannot tolerate these manipulations, because they are an affront to the very principle of democratic representation.
We'll beat them anyway!

I am not going to analyze the results province by province. I am sure that for you, Mr. Speaker, Alberta is very close to home. But as for Quebec, Quebec is losing four seats compared with what it had according to the Diefenbaker-MacEachen formula, already agreed to by all parties in the House and practically finalized, until the Conservative Government, partisan as always, brought in its own objectives.
Now this is a point that particularly concerns you, Mr. Speaker. As you know, you are responsible for appointing two commissioners in each province to monitor the readjustment of electoral boundaries. They are your responsibility. It is very important that these people be completely neutral, and that you can count on the impartial advice of your staff in appointing them and do not have to ask the Government to suggest candidates. You may be sure we intend to monitor the process very closely.
We have to ask ourselves what the Government's priorities are. I know the Conservative backbenchers don't even know the answer to that question. I am sorry that one of our House experts on the subject, the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis (Mr. Prud'homme), is not here-he is chairing a committee of the House that is discussing employment equity. But he would probably agree with us and say: Why are they giving this Bill priority? If adopting the amendments arising from the Budget is so urgent, if it is so terribly important to cut back and de-index family allowances, if it is so important to introduce a Bill presented by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) to reform divorce proceedings, and all kinds of other measures being insisted upon by the Government House Leader, why adjourn debate on the principle of the Bill for this kind of partisanship? Is it all that urgent? It is just a joke that the Government is asking for and imposing closure to hammer through all kinds of so-called important pieces of legislation- [English]
-after other matters which are more urgent.
Why is there priority given to this Bill when we are talking on third reading? Yesterday, when the Government came in with its seventh closure motion, we had enough. We used whatever legitimate facilities that were available to an opposition, outnumbered as we are in the House of Commons, to ensure that there be adequate debate and that the people of Canada, after hearing all sides of the question in the clash of that debate be able to form an opinion.
Yesterday, after two hours of debate at the report stage of the Bill to cut family allowance, notice of time allocation was proposed on this Bill for the second time. We are absolutely outraged because this is the Bill that deindexes the family allowances, takes away the protection from inflation for families, particularly those low and middle income families. It takes away that protection. In its arrogance, the Government has already printed the cheques and made them ready to mail in contempt of Parliament, before it has had a chance to discuss that Bill.
Shame.

Since October, the Government has invoked closure seven times. Let me cite for the record the Bills on which closure has been invoked. One is Bill C-62, concerning employment equity. I have mentioned Bill C-70 dealing with family allowance. Time allocation was imposed twice, once at second reading and once at the report stage. Another is the Bill we are discussing today. Bill C-74 dealing with electoral boundaries. Another is Bill C-79 with respect to depositors compensation. The Government imposes closure on the depositors compensation Bill when we do not even have the names of who we are paying. Parliament is being asked to give a blank cheque of up to $1 billion to people across the country whose names we do not even know.
Shame!

Closure was also imposed on Bill C-70, the Excise Tax Bill. Again, closure was imposed on Bill C-84, the Income Tax Act, the Bill which reflects the major provisions of the Budget. Those provisions are clear and include the personal surtax, the corporate surtax and the deindexation of the system. That is to say, every tax bracket has now been deindexed by 3 per cent per year and that means that we have the most massive, hidden increase in income tax in the history of this country. Four years from now, there will be an extra $11.5 billion in taxes collected from individual Canadians and the Minister did not have the guts to say that he was raising taxes.
As well, the Income Tax Bill contains the capital gains exemption which provides $500,000 over a lifetime for those wealthy or fortunate enough to be able to achieve on the disposition of an asset a capital gain. That benefit is not directed to-

speechtext: 1 will have to look at that. However, I would hope that the right hon. gentleman could continue.

Every tax expert in the country wants to talk about this Bill because it is a shambles. My friend, the Hon. Member for Saint-Henri-Westmount (Mr. Johnston), who is our Finance critic also happens to be a very reputable tax lawyer. He can tell us that there are now four tax codes in Quebec. There is the Quebec Income Tax Act, the federal Income Tax Act, the personal exemption for the $500,000 bonanza and the minimum tax. It will be an absolute shambles for the absolute taxpayer to try to understand what is happening.
I will list the Bills the Government wants passed by the end of the week. It wants Bill C-70, the Family Allowance Bill upon which it has imposed closure. That is the Bill that deindexes and cuts the family allowances. The Government wants Bill C-74, the Electoral Boundaries Bill which is before the House at the moment. It wants Bill C-79, the Depositors' Compensation Bill, that Blank cheque of $1 billion written to people we do not know. It wants Bill C-80, the Excise Tax Bill. It wants Bill C-83, the tax discounting Bill and it wants Bill C-84, the Income Tax Bill I have described, the main Budget Bill. That is what the Government wants in one delicious week. Have you ever heard anything like that before in your life, Mr. Speaker?
The Government justified imposing closure on the Income Tax Bill because it said that the Budget was introduced in May. The Bill containing the details of the Budget was only given to the House on November 26. It has only been before us for about two weeks. The most important bit of legislation to come before a free, democratic assembly annually has had closure imposed on it after only two weeks. The Government castrated the committee, limited discussion and refused the people of Canada the right to testify and give opinions.
Shame.

Mr. Speaker, you must be relieved that you are not a part of this gang and that you can sit here impartially and preside over a free assembly. Do you know what the House Leader wants in addition to all that?
He wants a vacation.
He needs a vacation. However, he wants a 64-page package of procedural reforms approved. We have studied these-
But you want to reform the House.

We're all for reform. In general terms, we like the report presented by the Hon. Member for St. John's East ably assisted by the Hon. Member for Papineau (Mr. Ouellet) and indeed the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie). They did a great job, but this 64-page package takes the best of the reform suggestions put by the Hon. Member for St. John's East and presents it to the House conveniently leaving out those procedures recommended by the Hon. Member that were not favourable to the

December 17, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
government side. If the report of the Hon. Member for St. John's East and the Hon. Member for Papineau were before us, we would take a look at it. However, this doctored, manicured, censored type of reform that the House Leader is bringing forward is a partisan, diluted document which we are not going to buy.
What about closure? 1 looked up the records regarding closure. It is a legitimate tool available to a Government. It is something that a Government can use from time to time but only after adequate debate.
That's a good trick.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: You should be picking these things up for your leader.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Is that what you do for Brian?

The Minister of Justice saw me drop my notes. If it had happened to him, he would not have been able to bend down to pick them up. In fact, he would have been well advised to leave them on the floor where they fell.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It's easy to amuse this crowd over here.
He and Pat Carney could have picked them up.
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, you offered me some good seats for the Grey Cup game and I appreciated that. Every once in a while, we have to hear from a few people from the bleachers. We need the Minister of Justice here to add a little comedy to the day.
The weapon of closure should only be used after adequate debate and after the issues have been thoroughly debated and presented to the people of Canada through Parliament so that the people can make a sane, cool, collected judgment on the merits of a piece of legislation.
Hear, hear!

This Government enjoys the largest majority in Canadian history: 211 Members against 30. For a Government with the largest majority in Canadian history having had to succumb to using closure seven times in the last five weeks is an admission of mismanagement and lack of competence.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, because I know you would want me to be fair I have reviewed the use of closure by Liberal Governments for the period 1969 to 1984. During those 15 years we used it on second reading 15 times. We used it in Committee of the Whole six times. We used it at report stage and third reading 11 times. At third reading only
we used it three times. That comes to a total of 35 times in 15 years.
This Government has used it seven times in five weeks. It is trying to use the pressure of the Christmas vacation to push this legislation through.
Hear, hear!
Mr. Speaker, because I want to be fair I will introduce some citations to the House, since there are some authorities sitting on the other side.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Are you going, John?
Is it getting to you, John? What happened to the old funnyman?
We have driven the Minister of Justice from the House.
Shame.

Mr. Speaker, have you ever noticed that those who can dish it out cannot take it? That is the way it is in life.
Let me recite the words of the House Leader who, then, was just the simple Member for Saskatoon West.
Still is!
I do not think that "simple" is unparliamentary. However, in the case of the House Leader it is devastatingly accurate.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You've brought back John.

Mr. Speaker, this is what the then Hon. Member for Saskatoon West said on the Crow debate. I wish to cite his remarks as reported in Hansard of May 16, 1983. Your Honour will recall that at this stage the Crow rate had been under review for about 18 months. These are the words of the Hon. Member for Saskatoon West:
Throughout the 18 months process of consultation leading up to the introduction of this legislation, the Opposition has been systematically excluded. We now find that on a piece of legislation of this importance the Government has seen fit to introduce closure after two days of second reading debate. I truly wonder about the state of our democracy and question whether the Government will be able to continue to call itself democratic in any way, shape or form.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Who said that?
That was Mr. Hnatyshyn, the Government House Leader.
Order.
After two days on second reading debate with respect to the Budget the Government introduced closure not 18 months ago but on November 16. Could we find more accurate and relevant words than those?

Hear, hear!

December 17, 1985
Mr. Speaker, where did Mr. Crosbie go?
Order.

He is gone again. The Minister of Justice is gone again. He is the Minister of Justice and the Hon. Member for St. John's West. In Hansard he is referred to as Mr. Crosbie. Sometimes when you are quoting directly from Hansard you can use the Hon. Member's name.
I would now like to quote from Hansard of April 2, 1981. These are the words of the Hon. Member for St. John's West:
Mr. Speaker, what we are now debating is another motion by a closure-crazy Government to close debate.
The Minister of Justice has had to swallow his words before and swallow his Party. He has crossed the floor three or four times in his life so that is not unusual for him.
Hear, hear!

Today, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mazankowski) was a little testy. We will deal with that in due course. I would like to say for the record that at the hearings of the committee relating to deregulation and to the report entitled "Freedom to Move", our members were in attendance about 95 per cent of the time. We resent very much what the Minister of Transport had to say about that.
Hear, hear!

This is what the Hon. Member for Vegreville had to say on July 7, 1981. It was with respect to the Crow debate. He said: "By virtue of a closure motion today, we have a further contempt for an erosion of the spirit and privileges of this institution." Those are memorable words. 1 did not think Maz was capable of it but they are tremendous words. He went on to say: "I believe tyranny begins when parliamentary debate ends."
That gets you right here, Mr. Speaker.
Hear, hear!
I could not have said it better. When this Government's short term comes to an end and the Minister of Transport is back to his automobile dealership I think we will hire him as a consultant.
As a speechwriter.

Mr. Speaker, I refer you to some remarks which the House Leader reputedly made to some journalists which I think affect the position of the Chair. I wish to draw them to the attention of the House. The House Leader told some journalists that if this package of legislation which he wants through before Christmas is not passed by the House he will call the House back during the normal time for the Christmas adjournment, perhaps as early as next week.
Representation Act, 1985
I wish to read to the Chair Standing Order 5 in this respect:
Whenever the House stands adjourned, if the Speaker is satisfied, after consultation with the Government, that the public interest requires that the House should meet at an earlier time, the Speaker may give notice that being so satisfied the House shall meet-
Thereby, of course, the House will have to come back earlier than the time set out in the rules. Not only is the House Leader repeatedly imposing closure, he is using the full force of his majority to stifle debate and, through his colleagues, he is keeping relevant and necessary documents from us. The President of the Treasury Board could have solved for himself a great many problems by tabling those necessary documents on the de Havilland deal.
Hear, hear!

The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Prime Minister could have helped the House and the country by tabling the necessary documents relating to free trade and where we are going. The Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) could have helped herself and the House by tabling the names of the uninsured, invisible depositors who will be the beneficiairies of a billion dollar bonanza. Thus, we have closure. We see the use of this immense majority and there is secrecy. We now have an implied threat by the House Leader that he wants to call us back next week.
Let me say to the House Leader, through you, Mr. Speaker, that that can only be done, under the Standing Order which I have just read, if the Speaker is satisfied, after consultation with the Government, that it is in the public interest so to do. It is your decision, Mr. Speaker. It is not the decision of the Government House Leader. I wish to say to Your Honour that you should not feel in any way embarrassed or intimidated by the House Leader because we are not.
Certainly not.
Hear, hear!

We are going to give Your Honour full support in applying this rule in the way in which it is meant to be applied.
Never in history has any Speaker used this authority, except in the case of a real national emergency, such as a paralysing transportation strike. None of the items on the list of the House Leader which I recited to the House, no matter how important, deal with an emergency in terms of application, time or in terms of their passage to warrant, in our submission to you, Your Honour's exercise of that judgment.
Right on.

Even the income tax legislation which affects the 1985 tax year does not fall into this category. In the past, income tax legislation has often been passed as late as the following February or March. If it had been so urgent to pass this piece of legislation, or the other measures which the Government has recited, why were they
9542

December i7, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
not brought to the House earlier? Why are we playing games with respect to redistribution? Why are we playing games with closure and secrecy and with using the great weight of the greatest majority in Canadian history?
The reason I am bringing this matter to your attention now, Mr. Speaker, is because under the rules you cannot be approached by the Government House Leader while the House is sitting. Standing Order 5 states that that can only be done after the House has adjourned. Only next week, or Friday midnight-whenever the House closes-will the House Leader be able to come to you. At that time we would not have an opportunity to make these arguments to you because the rule states "after consultation with the Government".
1 am submitting to you, Mr. Speaker, that the following are the precedents you ought to consider; in 1914 and 1939, when matters of the World War were to be considered, Parliament was not in session and special sessions were called. It was not just a recalling of an adjournment. There were Speeches from the Throne in those special sessions. The same held true in 1950; first, for the railway strike and, second for the Korean War. In 1956 there was a special session called to deal with the Middle East peace-keeping. Those were special sessions. Following are the cases where Parliament was recalled from an adjournment-the veiled threat of the House Leader- August 29, 1966, a railway strike; August 31, 1972, a grain-handlers' strike; August 30, 1973, a railway strike; August 9, 1977, an air traffic controllers' strike; and October 6, 1980, the consideration of a motion to establish a special joint committee of the Constitution. In the latter case, the House was recalled nine days early and the urgency was to get the committee underway before the delivery of the Budget, which was presented on October 28, 1980.
Debate on the Constitution, of course, was not a once in a lifetime matter, but it was the first time in more than a century a Canadian Parliament had been asked to begin so sweeping a change in our basic law. In any case, those citations relate to grave national emergencies, a paralysing transportation strike, grainhandlers' strike and an air traffic controllers' strike, something which goes to the daily convenience and public necessity of this country. Never has that rule been invoked by a Government House Leader, nor applied by a Speaker, just to accommodate the legislative program of the Government-never.
I see some relaxed faces opposite. Those Hon. Members do not want to come back after Christmas any more than anyone else. I say to you, Sir, it would be an amazing affront for the Government to attempt to put the Speaker into this invidious and embarrassing position, particularly when the Speaker has the role in this Parliament of protecting two minorities against the most overwhelming majority in Canadian history.
It may be well-and it is a matter between House Leaders-that some substantial progress can be made on the legislative program this week. However, if the Government continues to abuse the parliamentary system and if it continues to
apply the hammer, the closure, the limitation of debate, before we have had an adequate opportunity to review the legislation, then there will be no co-operation coming from this side. [Translation]
But I asked our House Leader to meet with his friend the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans), the House Leader of the New Democratic Party. There are possibilities to accommodate the Government and the Canadian people. But that could be done without the threat of an emergency session next week, without the threat of closure to limit opportunities for debate, without the massive weight of this Government's overwhelming majority.
Mr. Speaker, you know that all Members here have the right and the responsibility to scrutinize measures introduced in the House in the interest of all Canadians. With respect to family allowances, we are against the action of this Government because we want to protect low income families. We speak strongly against the lack of fairness when it comes to the capital gains tax exemption which favours the rich. We object on behalf of average families because at the same time the Government disregards fairness and upsets the balance of our Canadian parliamentary system.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that under the rules there is no opportunity to question the last speaker so I simply want to put two things on the record because I believe they should be put on the record. First, the last time allocation was used was for the debate on Monday, December 9, when Bill C-84, the important income tax Bill, was called. Bill C-84 was called for 11 o'clock in the morning. There was to be one day's debate. Debate was to finish at 4.45 p.m.
1 want to point out to the House that the Bill was called but there was no debate whatsoever on that day. In other words, when the day's debate was called, and the question was called, Hon. Members opposite who have complained so much about closure were not there to debate. Therefore, before anyone starts worrying about time allocation and abuse of democracy, they should realize that the abuse of democracy was when Hon. Members opposite were not there to debate the Bill which was called. The second point I want to put on the record-and I think probably the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) did this unintentionally-was when the electoral commissioners filed their reports in the last Parliament, which commissioners were appointed by the previous Liberal administration, it was my duty as the then Deputy House Leader to file the objections to the commissioner's report.
That's true.
Well, I want to go on the record for my Party that we never made any suggestion at that time that there was any gerrymandering of any riding.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: There wasn't.
There wasn't any.
There was never any suggestion that the boundaries of any of those ridings were politically misconstrued.
Thank you.
If those boundaries are fair, why are you changing them?
For that reason I think it is unfair and improper to either impugne the work of those commissioners-
No one is impugning your word.
-or to suggest that the commissioners who are going to be appointed under this Bill would follow any other course of action than to do what is right for the Canadian people.

Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to say a word or two in this debate. 1 want to begin by saying that much of what was said by the
Representation Act, 1985
Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) was absolutely correct. His analysis, if you will, of the pressure under which we are put as a result of the Government's use of time allocation is an accurate analysis. It is difficult for people to appreciate that the House of Commons, to a large extent, operates on the basis of goodwill, and goodwill is absolutely essential in the House of Commons if the House is to be able to do the necessary work which is expected of it by the people of Canada.
When the Government chooses-and I say this in this case to the Government across the way-to end debates prematurely by use of time allocation, the goodwill which is necessary becomes considerably lessened. That is true of this Government, and I say to the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition, who was not here during the immediately preceding Government, that it was equally true during the time of that Government.
I can remember the numerous times I rose in the House to ask the Government not to move on time allocation and to suggest that it was an inappropriate way to end debate. 1 want to say, however, in saying that, that I also believe, as I have said on many other occasions, that it is necessary for Hon. Members to be able to discipline themselves. It is necessary for Hon. Members not to simply use up the time of the House without giving due consideration to the over-all program which is before it. I believe it is the responsibility of all Hon. Members to look carefully at the program in front of us and to try to come to grips with the amount of time which may be necessary in order that that program can be adequately dealt with.
I am saying that I agree with what the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition has said regarding time allocation, particularly in the most recent past. Almost without exception on Bill after Bill it appears that the debate is being closed off. I admit it is not happening in every case but it certainly appears that every time the Government does not get its way it moves very quickly to use time allocation. Not only that, it will extend the sitting through the lunch hours so Bills can be rammed through. That is what causes the dissipation of goodwill which must exist in this House if we are going to do the necessary work. I want the Leader of the Official Opposition to appreciate that in the main I support his argument in that regard. I am, however, concerned about what has happened on this particular Bill.
I know that the Leader of the Opposition is fair-minded in this regard. It was very difficult for us, as the other opposition Party, to read the signals coming from the Liberal caucus. Very difficult. I say that in all fairness. It was hard for us to understand where the Liberal caucus was going on this Bill. My colleagues and I thought that the amendments offered were satisfactory. It was reported to us that the amendments met with the approval of the Liberal critic. They were in fact, in the main, the same amendments he had himself offered as being satisfactory. Therefore, it was difficult for us to suddenly

December 17, 1985
Representation Act, 1985
be faced with an uprising, if you will, after the process was finished. 1 would say this no matter what side of the House I was on. I am not trying to create a battle between us, I am simply telling the truth.
To go back to the beginning of this issue, we were given a paper to look at. My colleague from Churchill, who was a member of the committee, was unable to attend the initial meetings of that committee and 1 personally attended those meetings in order to be sure we were represented. The process had got to the point where in the final stages of the discussion of the redistribution Bill, when it got to committee, it was felt by most that it had been given reasonable amount of time. I would now be prepared to accept as true that what is being offered is unacceptable. I am not going to argue one side or the other at this point because it is too late in the debate. However, if that was true, if the amendment offered by the Opposition, which became the focal point for the Opposition as being unacceptable, was in fact unacceptable, then why in heaven's name did the Liberals offer it in the first place? That is my problem. Why argue for something and then, when you get it, turn it into a cause celebre to be used to defeat or stop passage of the Bill? I find that difficult to understand. I like to co-operate, damn it, and support what you are doing. 1 do support it. But I expect in return that there will be some consistency. If it had not been the intention of the Liberal Party to support the changes finally brought forward as amendments to the House, then they should not have offered them as amendments in the first place.
On top of all that, there would have then been a built-up Opposition. Surely it is not too much to ask that we be able to see where the points of opposition really lie so we can analyze them adequately and make some determination about their validity in order to come to grips with whether or not they are supportable. We were not given that opportunity. The committee worked itsway through and it was only after that, only after the recommendations came to the House having been agreed upon, that suddenly, without any warning, there loomed this massive opposition. To be perfectly frank I find that hard to deal with.
1 say now that we would have been perfectly willing to have considered any alternative scheme which was seen as satisfactory. My colleague would have brought that to our caucus, we would have looked it over, and gathered our forces to try and support it. That is all 1 ask. The process has within it at least three opportunities for debate. However, third reading is not where you start debating the process all over again. That is not where it happens. On third reading you may go back over the arguments you lost. You may want to state your continued opposition to what is happening. However, you do not reopen the entire process at third reading and expect that somehow or other everyone else is going to fall in line.
I say all that with the best of intentions and goodwill. I entirely agree with the attitude of the Leader of the Opposition regarding the way the Government has handled its business. However, I am personally perplexed that we find ourselves in the situation we are now in over this Bill. The Bill was
given broad discussion and this point of objection was never raised.
We never agreed to this.

1 am going by the record. If it was raised, it certainly does not appear as if it was. You can disagree with me and I will accept that we disagree on that. However, that is my sense of it, my reading and my understanding of it.
Having said that, let me say something about the Government. Members opposite said, when they ran for office, that they were going to be an open and forthright Government. They said they were going to deal upfront with what could and should be done in Parliament and in the country. Nothing could be further from the truth! There has been no greater disappointment over the last 15 months than this Government's continued attempts to not provide information to the House of Commons. At this moment we are debating two things and I think you will agree with me on this, Mr. Speaker. We are not only debating the content of the Bill, we are debating an atmosphere or mood which has developed over the last while.
Right.

We are trying to come to grips with it, find a way around it. However, going back as far as I can, every time we ask the Government to produce documentation to show conclusively how it arrived at the decisions it is taking, the Government has refused. Every single time. The Government says it is open. It says it is prepared to co-operate, to provide the documentation. However, on almost every single occasion that we asked for information regarding several issues over the last 15 months it has refused. I take you back not too far to the bank bail-out. Look at the tremendous problem we had in trying to arrive at an understanding over how the investigation would be undertaken. That was much like the position we are in again today. Here was the Government with a crisis on its hands and an Opposition-I was in on the negotiations- which said that it wanted to look at this objectively. Yes, also politically, I admit. That is, after all, what we are involved in. There is nothing wrong with looking at something from a political perspective; we are in fact in politics! Yes, we would anticipate differences of opinion will arise because of different ideologies as we view certain actions of the Government. However, all we asked in the bank bail-out situation was that we be given the relevant information. However, we had to drag it out inch by inch. We were refused at every turn. Every time we said: Can we have this document? No, you cannot get this document. Could we have that document? No, you cannot have that document. In the end all of the documents that we, in the House of Commons, asked to see have been presented to the Estey Commission-every single last bloody one of them. Now they are all public. However, would the Government be forthcoming and sufficiently trusting in the parliamentary process to provide the information to the House of Commons? Not likely. No, Sir. It could not do that. That was a bone of contention.
December 17, 1985

At that point I started to wonder about the forthrightness and openness of the Government. We were not asking for secret information. We were asking for the information the Government used to make a decision which will cost the taxpayers of Canada approximately $1 billion, which the Government neither committted itself to spending nor could have anticipated that it would spend. It was an extraordinary expenditure. I believe that we, in the Elouse of Commons, are entitled to know everything there is to know about the background material to support a request by the Government that it be allowed to spend $1 billion that it had not anticipated it would need to spend.
We said that the original bail-out and the subsequent collapse of the bank should be treated in the same way it would be if it were a bankruptcy. We said that those who wanted to make a claim should come forward and make it openly and be paid in accordance with whatever is available to pay them. That is the normal business practice.
Under the Winding-up Act.

That is the normal business practice and when we said that we should follow the normal business practice the Government looked at us as if we were mad. It said: "My good God, we cannot possibly tell you who is going to get the money". That is because the Government does not want to. It is not because there is any law against it or because there is any rule governing it. People tell me that the Bank Act does not allow it. This no longer falls under the Bank Act. That is the kind of thing which causes people to begin to withdraw from the co-operative spirit which is necessary to make the House of Commons operate effectively.
We then discovered that there are hundreds of millions of dollars that could be collected in taxes that are not being collected as a result of pre-tax rulings. We do not want to know anything about the people involved, but want to know how much is not being collected in order that we can come to grips with what this really means to the economy of Canada. Why is it that those who work for a living can be taxed at source but others can somehow work out fancy arrangements to save hundreds of millions of tax dollars without anyone understanding or knowing anything about it? We asked for some information with regard to that and the Government said: "Oh, no. You cannot have that. That is bad. You should know a thing like that". That is where we end up in that situation and it again undermines the very essence of co-operation that is so necessary for the House to operate.
We cannot, of course, get the details on de Havilland. We will get them if we ask the right questions every day.
Morsel by morsel.

The Leader of the Opposition says: "morsel by morsel". The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) says that he is giving us the answers. Let me assume for a
Representation Act, 1985
moment that he is. However, surely 1 do not have to sit up night after night every night of the week thinking up every conceivable question and asking it in the House of Commons to get to the bottom of the deal. That is outrageous and stupid. If the information was going to be given to me anyway, why can I not have the documents? That is all I am asking. I do not want to get into a personality battle over it. 1 understand that there may well be certain things which cannot be provided because of the delicate nature of the negotiations. I can appreciate that. I am not stupid, and neither are my colleagues. All we ask is to be treated in the way that we are intended to be treated by virtue of the fact that we ran for and got elected to Parliament. We are supposed to be trusted. We are supposed to be able to critically analyse the situation, not after the fact, but before the deal is completed.
I will close, Mr. Speaker, by saying that what is wrong in the House today is simply a lack of co-operation and a lack of understanding which I think the Government has fostered.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take the floor to comment briefly on the same
Cyprus
subject. I would suggest this problem has been with us for a long time and it does not seem it will be settled soon.
I have no difficulty with Motion No. 215 of the Hon. Member. I think his motion before the House is logical, but there was really no need to refer to the CAN DU reactor issue since it is the subject of a dispute which has nothing to do with the Island of Cyprus. I think the Hon. Member would have been better advised not to include that reference in his motion.
I think that the position of my Party and of the country in this debate... We believe the people of Cyprus must decide their own future and that there is no need at all-yesterday, today or tomorrow-to have the Turkish army intervene and have 40 per cent of the Cypriot territory occupied by the Turks.
The unilateral declaration of independence for the northern part of the Island of Cyprus has simply become a totally irrelevant element which does nothing to help matters. The problem ought to be resolved along the lines of the United Nations resolution which would enable all Cypriot citizens to express their views concerning the political solution of this problem which unfortunately has existed for a very long time.
Canada started to offer the services of Canadian Forces to keep peace in that country a long time ago. In my opinion, Canada's contribution to peacekeeping in that difficult situation which has prevailed for over twenty years on the Island of Cyprus should be made available to other parts of the world. And I think we should look at Cyprus and realize that U.N. intervention has to a considerable extent prevented loss of life and that the invasion that took place a few years ago proves that military intervention only makes matters worse instead of dealing with the problem, and that in the circumstances, Canada should continue to provide the services of its troops to keep the peace between the warring factions.
At this point, I believe I would say that I prefer Canada to intervene under the aegis of the UN, because when it is done at the invitation of the warring factions, we are making it impossible for the United Nations to maintain its credibility and intervene in an effective manner. Perhaps because the UN no longer has the prestige it enjoyed, let us say, 25 years ago countries are now intervening as the Turks did in the northern part of Cyprus, and we have seen the results. Thousands of people were displaced. Thousands of people have disappeared. Families want to know whether a person has disappeared or is in prison or what has happened to them. In the resolution, the Turkish Government is being asked to provide all the information they have on these individuals so that the human tragedy that has been going on since the intervention by the military can in some way or other be brought to an end.
Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to make a long speech. I think my party's position on the subject is well known, and 1 know

December 17, 1985
Cyprus
that the present Government's policy is not any different from the one we have supported to date. To clarify my position, perhaps I could read, for the benefit of the House, a short speech, a matter of minutes, which clearly established the Trudeau Government's position. Or perhaps I could simply refer the House to a speech made on November 17, 1983 by the Permanent Ambassador to the UN at the time, Mr. Gerard Pelletier, who clearly and succinctly summarized the Government's position. I could quote a few paragraphs that might be helpful to the people listening to this debate.
The Government's position was, and I believe it still is-and perhaps the Parliamentary Secretary will confirm this later on-that we profoundly regretted the unilateral declaration of independence on November 15 of the so-called Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus. We are not prepared to recognize this so-called state on Cyprus. We continue to recognize a single Republic of Cyprus, whose sovereignty and territorial integrity should be respected by all concerned. The unilateral declaration of independence has disrupted negotiations that are already delicate and difficult enough as it is. It is the unfortunate result of a situation previously described by the ambassador in June before the Council, that is, the two communities on Cyprus and certain other parties to the Cypriot dispute have not shown the requisite resolve to search for a compromise which, though difficult, will be necessary to find a valid political solution.
Although we are aware of the impatience and frustration felt by the parties as a result of the lasting stalemate, we cannot agree however that those sentiments warrant such a disproportionate reaction. The action of the Turkish Cypriot community jeopardizes chances for a fair and equitable solution within a unified Cypriot State, and for well deserved peace and prosperity.
Canada strongly deplores this unfortunate situation because our participation in the United Nations Force goes such a long way back. Indeed this force was created to maintain peace and pave the way for a solution to the Cypriot problem, not a unilateral solution but one which would be prepared and accepted by all parties concerned.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, it is a fair and reasonable position. The military intervention is not justified in these circumstances. We have to go back to the United Nations resolution and hope that the Cypriot problem will be solved by all the citizens of the Island of Cyprus in such a way that lasting peace might make people forget this unfortunate situation which has endured for too long but which, in my opinion and that of my Party, cannot be solved by a military intervention such as the one that took place on the Island of Cyprus.

speakeroldname: Mr. Chuck Cook (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS- MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF SUPPORTING UN RESOLUTIONS ON CYPRUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in my comments on this issue because there are two other Hon. Members who would like to speak in this debate and from
whom I would like to hear and, unfortunately, with the vote, there is not much time left. I will have a brilliant speech ready next time the Cyprus issue comes up. But it will not be this evening.
There are two or three points I would like to make. First, Canada's stand on Cyprus is not ambiguous at all. Our efforts have always aimed at helping the peace process and facilitating the UN Secretary-General's efforts. Second, Canada regrets deeply such actions as the 1974 foreign interventions or the 1983 unilateral Declaration of Independence. Third, Canada has supported resolutions aiming at the withdrawal of foreign military personnel on Cyprus except those provided for in the Cyprus Constitution.
The UN Secretary-General is actively pursuing his efforts to reconcile the two communities. Any unsolicited and one-sided action by Canada at this delicate point of the discussions would undermine his initiative and be counter-productive. In his recent speech at the Fortieth United Nations General Assembly, the Cyprus Foreign Minister called for all to support the Secretary-General and to "assist him in finding a solution to the problem". The motion presented today does not seem likely to have such effect.
Canada is a key member of the United Nations force in Cyprus. Its contingent patrols the most sensitive sector of the "green line". While Canada itself recognizes only the Republic of Cyprus, the Canadian contingent must maintain its credibility in the eyes of the Turkish as well as the Greek Cypriots. The adoption of this motion could raise questions as to Canadian impartiality as peace-keepers.
The lives of 25 Canadian servicemen have been lost in Canada's efforts to bring peace to the country of Cyprus. Tens of millions of Canadian dollars have been spent in our peacekeeping efforts over the years. Passing this motion would undermine that impartiality which Canada must maintain if we are to have a loud and clear voice in bringing peace to that troubled island.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS- MOTIONS   EXTERNAL AFFAIRS ADVISABILITY OF SUPPORTING UN RESOLUTIONS ON CYPRUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me again point out that Canada has many years of experience in Cyprus and that its position has been carefully elaborated over the years. We feel that under the circumstances, this position is the one most likely to help the Secretary-General of the United Nations who has been mandated to bring about a reconciliation in Cyprus. The Cypriot question is a very complex one. Not only is it the result of many centuries of sometimes difficult cohabitation between Greek and Turkish Cypriots, but it is also a product of the often violent relations between two peoples whose language, religion and culture differ considerably.
The vagaries of history kept Cyprus from becoming part of Greece like other islands in the Aegean and Mediterranean in the nineteenth and twentieth century, and in 1878, Cyprus came under the control of Great Britain. Nevertheless, there is
December 17, 1985

still a profound attachment to the Greek language and culture and to the Greek Orthodox religion. At the same time, a Turkish presence on the island since the 15th century had produced a cohesive and strong minority, 18 per cent, with strong ties to the Turkish language and culture and to Islam. [English]
We are all familiar with the painful process which led to the independence of Cyprus. Hellenism has been there for a long time but not until 1931, it is felt, was a desire for enosis, uniting Cyprus with Greece, expressed with any seriousness. After the war Britain began to decolonize and grant independence to its colonies one by one. A campaign in favour of enosis, accompanied by terrorist attacks against British interests, was launched in Cyprus in 1955. The Turkisk Cypriots, fearing abandonment by England, tried to resist the pressure for enosis and independence and called for the maintenance of the status quo or, failing that, partition of the island. They finally agreed with the Greek Cypriots on a draft constitution in which the right of the minority were protected. Moreover, when independence was achieved, Cyprus signed with London, Ankara and Athens a treaty which gave the three countries the right to inspect implementation of the agreements. The institutions put in place in 1960 by the Zurich and London agreements have not worked. The Turkish Cypriots claim that they have systematically been excluded from important decisions and that their rights have not been respected, while the Greek Cypriots contend that the Turkish Party has refused to cooperate and abused its veto powers.
We do not have the time to review in this House the many events which have marked the past 21 years. In 1964 civil war was raging and the Government of Cyprus, having consulted with the three guarantor states, appealed to the United Nations. Canada has witnessed most of these events. From 1964 through 1974 Canadian soldiers, like their counterparts from other contributing countries, were assigned to positions in the cities, towns and villages where Greek and Turkish Cypriots were fighting. Their main job was to keep the peace, prevent fresh outbreaks of fighting and create conditions conducive to reconciliation.
After the events of 1974 the Island was divided in two. The UN force was re-deployed along the cease-fire line. The Canadian troops were given the difficult mission of patrolling the old sector of Nicosia where the enemy positions are sometimes only a street's width apart and where the presence of many buildings in ruins makes it very difficult to exercise surveillance over the fortifications and the cease-fire line.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, before I go on with my speech, I must pay a well-deserved tribute to those 23,000 young Canadians who, with dignity and courage, have performed an extremely dangerous and I would say frustrating task. It is inspiring to see these soldiers and officers, trained to defend their country against the enemy and if necessary, attack that enemy, acting as referees between opponents whose motivation and courage make them formidable fighters.
Cyprus

One's concept of the role played by the UN force in Cyprus can vary depending on one's own perception of things. This international force, which has numbered as much as 6,800 and is now 2,340 strong, has not always been able to prevent skirmishes from degenerating into widespread combat. It was powerless in the face of the events of 1974. As I said, there must be a reciprocal political desire before the UN force can fulfil its mission. However, many of the soldiers could testify to the lives they have saved, the supplies they have brought to isolated villages, and the hundred of refugees whom they have led to a safe zone. Many times they have passed from one zone to another bringing mail, helping isolated family members visit one another, and watching over the aqueduct work in Nicosia which is proceeding without regard for the Green Line. In short, they are maintaining against all obstacles a state of peace and communications which will enable the political leaders and the UN representatives to continue the dialogue. These soldiers could also tell you about the long nights and days they have spent patrolling the cease-fire line between two rows of fortifications strewn with death-traps. These Canadians are professional soldiers and are always on the look-out for attempts by either side to strengthen an outpost or a barricade, or to move a portion of the cease-fire line. They are also diplomats who, on behalf of the UN, negotiate with each party to resolve initiatives or misunderstandings which might change the status quo and precipitate a confrontation. In 1984 only one life was lost along this line. In 1985, none. Those who feel these troops need not be there have only to imagine what would happen if they were withdrawn or even if their numbers were reduced.
Others feel that Canada is not doing enough. Earlier on, when I mentioned the cost of Canadian participation in this peace-keeping force, I left out what it costs Canada indirectly to send these troops to Cyprus rather than keep them here. Consider also that the services provided by the soldiers are not available to the Canadian people, so that the total cost, not always quantifiable, is actually higher than it appears to be. In sum, those who would like to see Canada take a position on the actions of the parties involved need only ask our soldiers what effect this would have on their ability to keep the peace. I would also ask them to reflect on the effects this motion would have on the mediatory work being done by the UN Secretary-General since the summer of 1984, to mention only the most recent of his initiatives. The Cypriot communities, as well as the Greek and Turkish Governments, recently reiterated their confidence in the Secretary-General's efforts. He earnestly desires to see each party negotiate seriously, with no outside interference and with a willingness to once and for all re-establish the minimal confidence required to produce valid concessions. The two Cypriot communities seem to agree on the principle of setting up a federal state. Yet to be determined is the exact nature of this state, the reciprocal rights each part would have, and the guarantees which would ensure the survival of this federal state and the security of its citizens.

December 17, 1985
Adjournment Debate

Because they are so far removed from Cyprus, Canadians have trouble understanding what is at stake in a situation that has existed for over 20 years. However, they do realize that any definitive failure of the UN's efforts in Cyprus would have devastating consequences, not only for the Cypriots but for the world community and world peace.

Before it is too late we must lend all the support we can to the only person who has a chance to bring the two communities back to the negotiating table and keep them there. For the sake of future generations, patience and confidence must be evident among all involved. Threatening or inflammatory declarations, and attempts by the parties to strengthen their positions by drawing the international community into the conflict, are contrary to the objectives of Mr. Perez de Cuellar and the methods he would see used. For its part, Canada will continue to support with all its resources and prestige the multilateral approach to finding a solution. It will, if asked, continue to lend assistance in the field and quietly encourage the parties involved. In this way, and not by passing motions like the one before us, we will best contribute toward a just and appropriate solution to the problems of Cyprus.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 46 deemed to have been moved.

Mr. Speaker, on November 27 I wanted to ask the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) a question about tax reform. In his absence, I asked the question of the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall). In my question I indicated how confused Canadians are about our tax system and how disappointed they are, and I used other adjectives as well. I did not consider the reply I got to be totally satisfactory. I would now like to outline some of my further thoughts on this vital topic in Canada.
I had the privilege of visiting Washington last spring with a number of colleagues to study the important issue of tax reform. I found it a very worthwhile meeting. As you know, President Reagan has set tax reform as a very, very high priority of his administration and the Americans are moving along that path. It is not easy. We saw several different versions of the so-called minimum tax and flat-rate tax in the United States. However, I believe they have the will and determination to follow through with that. I am confident that we will see the same determination in our country. The Prime
Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has said that we will move along that path and I think it is time we got that process underway.
I would like to talk about a few of the problems with our current system and give a few examples of it. 1 attended the meeting of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs last evening at which we dealt, clause by clause, with Bill C-84. I will give you just one example of an amendment which we were considering. It reads:
(B) the corporation is, throughout the year, a Canadian-controlled private corporation whose taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year together with the taxable incomes of all corporations with which it was associated in the year for their taxation years ending in the calendar year immediately preceding the calendar year in which the taxation year of the corporation ended does not exceed the aggregate of the business limits (as determined under section 125) of the corporation and the associated corporations for those preceding years, or"
That is just one example, Mr. Speaker, of the complexity of the Income Tax Act.
With great respect to several of the architects of that Act over the years, I think we have ended up with a band-aid solution. There has been change after change after change. I would defy any tax lawyer or tax accountant in the country to try to comprehend that entire Act. The provision which the Government is moving forward with through the last Budget, the lifetime capital gains exemption of $500,000, is a proposal which I personally feel is a good one. However, as we discussed Bill C-84, that one proposal alone touched on over 130 parts of the Act. Therefore, you can see the complexity of it.
Individuals, as well as companies, have a hard time filling in tax returns. Many of them have given up and have had to go to various tax preparation companies. I think that in itself speaks to the unnecessary complexity of the law.
As the Government deals with tax reform, I believe it should move ahead on the basis of revenue neutrality. In other words, Canadians should not perceive that we are changing the tax provisions just to get more taxes into the Treasury of the country. When we do embark on this in a serious way we should follow the principle of revenue neutrality. When the total changes are made, the Government collects the same amount of money.
Some of the things we should be thinking about and considering, which I call important principles, include the current minimum tax. It has a principle in it, to which I object, having to do with the gross-up of dividends on which people are being taxed. 1 do not think Canadians should be taxed on money they do not receive.
As we review this whole topic we should look at a consolidated return for corporations. With my business background, I recall when one deals with the acquisition or selling of a company that the first area to be explored is that of the tax consequence. You do not look at the market-place, how long the company has been in business or what the sales force is like, you look at what the tax situation is. Is there a tax loss carry forward? It is almost like a shell game when annual returns are filed, Mr. Speaker, shifting assets into different
December 17, 1985

companies so tax can be minimized. A simple thing, like a consolidated tax return, as they have in the United States, would go a long way toward that very point.
I have a number of other points 1 want to make on this issue, but let me conclude by saying that as we embark on this important initiative we must ensure that Canadians perceive it as being fair and equitable. They do not at this stage. We have something in the order of over 25,000 employees in Revenue Canada in the excise area-I do not want anybody to lose his or her job-which speaks of the mammoth job at hand, while we have over 12 million people trying to fill out returns. I submit our system is far too complex. We need to get on with strong backing and a strong initiative on tax reform in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Pierre H. Vincent (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, our Government has shown that it takes the development of a fair and efficient tax system seriously by introducing and proposing a number of initiatives on this issue. These continuing series of steps considered in aggregate represent major advances in fairness.
One of the first actions taken by the Government was to put an end to the abuses of the quick flip mechanism associated with the scientific research tax credit. These abuses by certain individuals and corporations had resulted in a significant loss in revenue for the treasury.
The Government has implemented a number of reforms in the area of tax administration. The November 1984 economic statement introduced measures designed to improve the fairness of tax administration. These measures include requiring a taxpayer to be refunded any overpayment of income tax resulting from a successful appeal-even if under further appeal-restricting the authority of officials for search and seizure, to be consistent with the spirit of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. The Government does not believe in being Draconian in its pursuit of the tax dollar, and has made changes to humanize the tax collection process.
The May 23 Budget contained a number of proposals directed toward increasing the fairness of the Canadian tax system. Measures relating to these proposals were tabled in the House with the November 21, 1985 Notice of Ways and Means Motion. Two major measures relating to fairness between taxpayers are the restriction on use of the capital cost allowance losses from certain types of businesses for individuals, and the extension of the income attribution rules to income from property acquired from the proceeds of interest-free loans.
In an effort to prevent tax avoidance, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced on November 26, 1985 a measure to prevent the use of trusts to market security issues in a way that income and capital returns to investors are distributed tax free.
On December 4, 1985 a major step was taken when the minimum tax legislation was introduced. It guarantees that
Adjournment Debate
high income individuals will not escape paying income tax. In addition, on the same day, the Minister of Finance introduced measures ending the use of partnerships in corporate takeovers for increased tax deductions and clarifying the law on the limits imposed on foreign property investments by pension funds. These measures are designed to make the tax system more fair and to safeguard federal revenue.
