subtopic: FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-MAINTENANCE OF QUOTAS-(A) GOVERNMENT POSITION (B) REQUEST THAT QUOTAS BE RETAINED
FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-MAINTENANCE OF QUOTAS-(A) GOVERNMENT POSITION (B) REQUEST THAT QUOTAS BE RETAINED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 23 I put a question to the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens), asking him to act responsibly and maintain quotas in the footwear industry. Now we know that the Government decided to eliminate the quotas, and immediately afterwards, Mr. Speaker, I went to my riding, the riding of Saint-Leonard-Anjou, which has three shoe factories employing 1,000 workers. One of the comments made by the shoe manufacturers in my riding and which they asked me to take down was that, in fact, the worker stands to lose by this decision, because the manufacturers can go on designing Canadian shoes here and have them manufactured in Brazil and then import them into Canada, which they can do because there are no more quotas.
Mr. Speaker, that is the situation at the present time. These are jobs that have been lost as a result of this decision. In fact, Mr. Speaker, this has been confirmed by a report from ILO, which says that eighteen industrialized countries are now experiencing increased job losses in the footwear industry as a result of imports from developing countries.
Mr. Speaker, this indeed confirms statements by manufacturers who intend to stay in business despite the fact the quotas have been lifted. They are going to have the shoes manufactured in developing countries, but our workers, our Canadian workers are going to lose their jobs.
Mr. Speaker, workers in the Canadian footwear industry as well as manufacturers, tanners and suppliers are very disappointed and even concerned, not only because of this Government's very poor policy on import quotas on shoes but also because of the specious arguments invoked since then in the House to justify the Government's decision.
Manufacturers and workers are asking the following question: Why is the Government trying to mislead the House and the public by pointing out that the quotas have cost consumers between $450 million and $500 million? Why does it refer to figures from a theoretical study without taking into consideration the way the shoe market operates or the real price of shoes? Why does it use overestimated figures based on an

December 17, 1985
Adjournment Debate
econometric evaluation-not to mention projections for the years 1984 and 1985-yet fail to mention that, according to the Tribunal, econometric evaluation procedures give results which can never be considered to be totally accurate? Why does it not keep Members aware of that? Why does the Tribunal refer to figures based on an econometric evaluation whose results cannot be considered to be totally accurate?
The Government knew that it was because the Tribunal was unable to obtain figures from retailers and importers, as it indicated in its report. Why did the Government fail to advise the House about what the Tribunal said concerning the price consumers have to pay for shoes?
I could go on, Mr. Speaker, and say that Canadians deserve more than mere theoretical studies. They deserve to know the truth because 20,000 workers will be affected by this decision.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I would like just for the record to quote the promise made on May 4, 1984 by the Right Hon. the Prime Minister, who was then Leader of the Opposition. Here is an article from the newspaper La Tribune:
On Wednesday Conservative Leader Brian Mulroney told the daily newspaper La Tribune that a Conservative Government would not abolish import quotas imposed by Canada in the footwear and textile sectors.
"The quota policy would remain unchanged", said Mr. Mulroney because he is not in favour of free-trade in those sectors.
He added that he would not give in in spite of pressures that might be applied by the Common Market countries or the United States to loosen quotas on shoes or textile products in Canada.
"I will not miss the opportunity to say so to President Reagan when 1 confer with him in Washington next month. I will see to it that our interests are protected at all times. A friendship has its price. Neighbours like us are worth a lot", said the Conservative Leader.
What a joke, Mr. Speaker! After 15 months in office he abolishes quotas, yet on May 4, 1984 he had clearly stated he would maintain them, even in spite of pressures from the Americans and the European Common Market.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Monique Landry (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
subtopic: FOOTWEAR INDUSTRY-MAINTENANCE OF QUOTAS-(A) GOVERNMENT POSITION (B) REQUEST THAT QUOTAS BE RETAINED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to answer the question raised by the Hon. Member for Saint-Leonard-Anjou (Mr. Gagliano) on October 23, 1985, and to refer to the decision taken by the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) and announced in the House of Commons on November 20, 1985 concerning the Government's future policy on shoe imports.
In his announcement the Minister mentioned the Canadian Import Tribunal report which had been commissioned by the previous administration and according to which the Canadian shoe industry, with the exception of shoes for women and young girls, can compete successfully on international markets. In light of the tribunal findings, the Government came to the conclusion that it would not be in the best interests of the country to continue to restrict imports throughout the whole industry.

Accordingly, effective December 1, 1985, import controls are being continued for a further three years only with respect to women's and girls' dress and casual footwear. Quotas for this sector will be phased out to annual growth provisions of 6 per cent the first year, 8 per cent the second year and 10 per cent the third year.
The Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelleher) stressed that adjustment assistance programs would be available for communities, employees and companies. Furthermore, the industry currently benefits from a tariff of around 23 per cent on footwear imports and will continue to have recourse to the provisions of the Special Import Measures Act.

subtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-HOUSING PROJECT IN SACKVILLE, N.S.
CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-HOUSING PROJECT IN SACKVILLE, N.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to explain further the gross error of the present Government as well as the previous Government in regard to the shell housing program in places like Sackville, Nova Scotia. About 1972 there were a number of houses built. At least 23 have been identified as having trouble now, in which the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation approved the contractors who constructed the shell and then the shell was sold to the customer-the homeowner-to-be-who is responsible for completing the interior work.
CMHC approved the whole arrangement and approved the contractors. CMHC was responsible for inspecting the houses. The people who bought the houses and are living there yet say that there was no inspection until the end. In the end, the inspector came around, drove up in his car, met with the builder who drove up in his truck or car, but did not go into the house, and signed the inspection documents. In other words, they covered for the fact that he had not inspected it. As I say, this was done under the jurisdiction and with the approval of CMHC. It turns out that the roof was very badly designed. It was designed in such a way that it was bound to rot for lack of ventilation. On one street, 23 of the roofs of that design and construction are rotting in that way. One has already fallen in and others have had to be replaced so that they would not fall in. After complaints that began in 1974 and 1975, it took the Government until 1985 to do anything about it, whichever Government was in power.
The fact is that CMHC was responsible from start to finish, up to the point where the project was handed over to the unsuspecting home owners who foolishly trusted a government body to tell them they were buying sound houses. The present Government has treated them almost as shabbily as the previous Government which produced the bad housing.
Some of the home owners have had to double the amount of their mortgages in their later years in order to fix houses which were faulty when they were sold to them under the jurisdiction and direction of CMHC. Some extra rehabilitation money has
December 17, 1985

been given but it amounts to no more than $2,000 per house for roofs which cost $10,000, $15,000 or $18,000. They should have been fixed before and should not have been charged to the home owners at all. It is the responsibility of CMHC.
The Minister promised to report on this situation to a local Member of the Legislature but repeatedly refused to forward that promised report. His words were that he expected to be able to provide the Member of the Legislature with the results of his investigation by early June. It is December and there is no report. My office requested this report by letter on November 26, by phone on November 26 and December 2, by letter on December 6, in a speech on December 10, in a question on December 12 and in phone calls Friday, Monday and today, and never once did the Minister respond to the request for a report, let alone make the report public.
Clearly the Minister responsible for CMHC is as ashamed to report on the matter as he would have been if he had been the Minister responsible at the time this disgraceful building project was created. The Government has inherited all the power, prestige and revenues of the previous Government and it inherited with that its debts, both legal and moral, of which this certainly is one. The Government owes new roofs to the owners of those houses in Sackville and if it slides out of providing those roofs it is defaulting on a moral obligation and that will bring disgrace to the Government.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Price (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: CANADA MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION-HOUSING PROJECT IN SACKVILLE, N.S.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member suggested that the Minister and his staff members have a lack of sensitivity or have shown a lack of co-operation. I should remind the Hon. Member, as he certainly knows, that the Minister does indeed take the Hon. Member's representations very seriously and that the Minister and the members of his staff have responded to his inquiries very promptly. As an example, today members of the Minister's staff were, as they were on many other occasions, in contact with the Hon. Member's staff to assist the Hon. Member in his endeavours on behalf of the people he represents.
I would like to respond further to the matter raised by the Hon. Member which, of course, concerns the problems being experienced by the homeowners in a housing project in
Adjournment Debate
Sackville, Nova Scotia. The project in question consists of some 22 semi-detached units which were built in the early 1970s as part of a joint federal-provincial program known as shell housing. The basic idea underlying the program was to bring housing units to a stage of construction which permitted occupancy. The owner occupants then completed the work creating equity in the properties at the time of completion. Under the program, CMHC provided loans to builders who were responsible for the shell of the units and to persons with a previously agreed income at an agreed maximum price.
The problem of deterioration in some of the units was brought to the attention of CMHC earlier this year. As a result of that representation an inspection was carried out which found that in some of the units rotting had occurred due to moisture entering the roof system. Contrary to the Hon. Member's suggestion, these observations have been communicated to the Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) who, I might add, has made representations to the Minister on behalf of his constituents. As well, these observations have been made known to the local MLA, Mr. Holm.
The actual report was produced for CMHC internal use and, as such, is not a document for public consumption.
The federal Government has no liability in this matter. However, despite that, CMHC has undertaken to do its utmost to respond to the needs of these homeowners within the parameters of existing programs. Many of the occupants have considerable equity in their homes and, where feasible, CMHC will work with lenders and the homeowners to extend mortgages to cover the costs of repair. In the case of hardship, CMHC is prepared to arrange adjustments to loan repayment terms. CMHC has also reallocated available funds in the Residential Rehabilitation Assistance Program to Halifax County for this project.
